items.originalTitle: Norway should buy OpenAI
items.summary:
A proposal argues that Norway’s Government Pension Fund Global, valued at over $2 trillion, should purchase OpenAI, currently valued around $800 billion, to bring the AI lab under public control and ensure its benefits serve humanity broadly. The argument highlights concerns about AI’s rapid advancement outpacing institutional responses, the concentration of power and wealth in private hands, and the risks posed by unregulated AI development.

The proposal notes OpenAI’s origins as a capped-profit nonprofit with commitments to public benefit, which were later abandoned, and suggests Norway’s stable democracy and internationalist stance make it a suitable steward. It recommends that after acquisition, management could be transferred to an international multilateral institution. The proposal acknowledges potential political obstacles, especially from the U.S., but frames the move as a necessary intervention to address the social and economic challenges posed by AI automation and concentration of AI-related wealth and power.

items.originalTitle: GLM-5.3 Artificial Analysis Benchmarks
items.summary:
ArtificialAnalysis.ai released detailed benchmarks for the proprietary GLM-5.3 model in August 2026, highlighting its strong performance on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index with a score of 60, well above the median of 35. The model supports text input and output with a 1 million token context window and is moderately priced at $1.40 per million input tokens and $4.40 per million output tokens.

The evaluation covered 181 models in the same class, comparing intelligence, speed, cost, and verbosity. GLM-5.3 demonstrated high verbosity with 170 million generated tokens during testing, significantly above the median of 72 million. The total cost to run the intelligence index evaluation on GLM-5.3 was $1,238.50. The benchmarks also include various intelligence subtests such as reasoning, coding, knowledge, and hallucination rates, providing a comprehensive performance profile for this reasoning-capable model.

items.title: Linear reports AI adoption doubled across all software team functions in first half of 2026, with nearly half of issues now AI-authored [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: AI usage patterns in software teams
items.summary:
Linear analyzed AI usage patterns within its software development platform from January to June 2026, finding that AI adoption more than doubled across all team functions, including product and go-to-market roles. Executives, including CEOs at larger companies, showed significant increases in AI use, and adoption was consistent regardless of company size. AI now authors nearly half of all issues created in Linear, and pull requests have increased by 111% since mid-2024, driven largely by coding agents.

The study also found that teams are spending more time creating, triaging, and commenting within Linear, with new AI-related activities such as chatting with AI and delegating tasks to AI agents emerging alongside existing workflows. Non-engineering roles like product managers and designers are increasingly contributing code, indicating a shift toward broader participation in software delivery. Despite these changes, planning time within Linear remained steady, suggesting AI has so far impacted execution more than decision-making in product development.

The effort focuses on helping these institutions keep pace with AI's rapid adoption in security contexts while ensuring accountability and transparency.

The initiative includes $5 million in funding for training and technical support, development of interoperable tools to help authorized reviewers understand AI-assisted government decisions, and collaboration with civil society and technical experts. OpenAI emphasizes that oversight responsibility remains with elected officials and public institutions, and its role is to support these bodies in fulfilling their mandates effectively.

items.title: Google Says Its AI Can Do the Work of Forward Deployed Engineers [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Google Says Its AI Can Do the Work of Forward Deployed Engineers
items.summary:
Following the playbook Palantir pioneered, OpenAI, Anthropic, Microsoft and Amazon are investing billions of dollars to hire so-called forward deployed engineers to get newfangled AI to work in enterprises. 

Then there’s Google, which says AI can automate some of what these FDEs do. 

While Google Cloud recently said it plans to hire hundreds of FDEs to help customers figure out what kind of apps they want to develop with its Gemini AI tools, the company is now automating some of the work these specialized consultants do for large companies to organize their data, said Andi Gutmans, a Google Cloud vice president and general manager who oversees its database products.

Until recently, FDEs worked on-site with customers to organize proprietary corporate data to ensure AI could make better sense of it and thus help employees analyze it faster and more accurately. For instance, businesses often define financial metrics such as gross revenue differently, and the FDE’s manual work aimed to ensure the AI would understand such differences.

Gutmans said that Google has realized the limits of this labor-intensive approach. “If you want to move to activating 100% of your enterprise data, you're not going to be able to hire enough people to make that happen,” he said. 

In his view, customers can get the most value from AI agents by giving them access to as much data as possible, including their files and legal contracts. Google’s AI-powered FDEs scour through customers’ data to understand how it relates to various parts of their business operations, like sales and inventory management.

The Mojo programming language has been promising an open source release since May 2023. Last week they shipped their 1.0 and today they have followed through on that original promise, releasing the compiler and toolchain under an Apache 2 license.

When Mojo first launched the stated goal was to produce a superset of Python, so existing Python code could be used to bootstrap their own ecosystem. That plan changed around August 2025:

Mojo may or may not evolve into a full superset of Python, and it’s okay if it doesn’t.

We’re encouraged by how well AI-assisted coding tools already help migrate Python to Mojo today, and we’re confident that future tooling and ecosystem maturity will make this evolution even smoother.

Today Mojo is its own language, optimized to make GPU programming as painless as possible using syntax inspired by Python, if not 100% compatible with existing code.

items.title: How to Prepare for Trademark Filing Using Google Gemini [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: How to Prepare for Trademark Filing Using Google Gemini
items.summary:
Starting a new business requires founders to make important decisions and tackle complex processes in areas where they typically lack expertise, such as human resources and accounting.

One of the most important early steps is filing for a trademark to protect your brand name, logo, and other identifying assets from unauthorized use. Trademark registration can help you enforce your legal rights, but the filing process often involves unfamiliar terminology and strict adherence to detailed processes.

Google Gemini can help you get up to speed on the basics of filing a trademark, evaluate attorneys, and prepare for the entire filing process.

Step 1: Make a Plan

Decades ago, founders would need to buy niche business books or visit a law library to learn what goes into filing a trademark. Even just a few years ago, the learning process would likely take hours of web research, requiring you to peruse one site after another, slowly piecing together the puzzle as you tried to determine which sources were the most credible.

Today, Gemini can give you an on-demand crash course. Open a new chat and type: What is the step-by-step process for filing a trademark, and what are the typical timelines?

Gemini will outline the major steps—including a preliminary clearance search (checking to make sure your desired trademark isn’t already in use), application preparation and filing, examination by the United States Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO), publication, and registration—along with an estimated timeline for each.

This overview will help you set realistic expectations and prepare for the process ahead.

Step 2: Prepare Questions for Your Lawyer

Chances are, you won’t be filing your trademark application completely on your own. Many founders rely on an experienced attorney to help them streamline the process and navigate obstacles.

Before you meet with an attorney for the first time, let Gemini help you prepare a set of relevant questions that will help you make a more informed decision.

Try this prompt:

I am preparing to hire a trademark attorney to clear and file a trademark for my business, [Insert Business Name/Niche]. What questions should I ask a trademark attorney during an initial consultation?

Gemini might suggest asking about the lawyer’s expertise in your specific industry, how he or she conducts clearance searches, and fee structures. If there are additional topics you want to explore, you can run them by Gemini for follow-up suggestions.

Step 3: Translate Legal Jargon

Trademark law is full of highly specific, nuanced terms that may be unfamiliar to most founders. When you come across one of these legal terms, Gemini can help explain it in plain language. Here’s an example prompt:

Explain the concept of “Likelihood of Confusion” in trademark law as if I am a business owner with no legal background. What does “likelihood of confusion” mean, and how do trademark examiners evaluate it?

In this case, Gemini may explain that a trademark application can be rejected even if it is not 100% identical to an existing trademark, as long as consumers might mistakenly believe that your products or services are being delivered by an existing company.

Step 4: Organize Your Materials

You want to make your trademark attorney’s job as simple as possible for two reasons: 1) When your attorney has all relevant assets, accurate information about your products and services, and clear examples of how the mark is being used, it reduces the odds of misunderstandings and paves the path for a smoother application process; and 2) Most lawyers bill by the hour.

Instead of spending the first 30 minutes of your consultation digging through your files, take a moment to gather and organize materials beforehand. Gemini can help.

Try this prompt: I am preparing for my first meeting with a trademark attorney. Create a checklist of the exact business assets, dates of first use, URLs, and brand materials I need to gather beforehand so I don’t waste billable hours.

By putting in this preparation work at the beginning of the process, you can avoid delays, reduce unnecessary legal fees, and ultimately secure the trademark protection you need to build a lasting business.

Decades ago, founders would need to buy niche business books or visit a law library to learn what goes into filing a trademark. Even just a few years ago, the learning process would likely take hours of web research, requiring you to peruse one site after another, slowly piecing together the puzzle as you tried to determine which sources were the most credible.

Today, Gemini can give you an on-demand crash course. Open a new chat and type: What is the step-by-step process for filing a trademark, and what are the typical timelines?

Gemini will outline the major steps—including a preliminary clearance search (checking to make sure your desired trademark isn’t already in use), application preparation and filing, examination by the United States Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO), publication, and registration—along with an estimated timeline for each.

This overview will help you set realistic expectations and prepare for the process ahead.

Step 2: Prepare Questions for Your Lawyer

Chances are, you won’t be filing your trademark application completely on your own. Many founders rely on an experienced attorney to help them streamline the process and navigate obstacles.

Before you meet with an attorney for the first time, let Gemini help you prepare a set of relevant questions that will help you make a more informed decision.

Try this prompt:

I am preparing to hire a trademark attorney to clear and file a trademark for my business, [Insert Business Name/Niche]. What questions should I ask a trademark attorney during an initial consultation?

Gemini might suggest asking about the lawyer’s expertise in your specific industry, how he or she conducts clearance searches, and fee structures. If there are additional topics you want to explore, you can run them by Gemini for follow-up suggestions.

Step 3: Translate Legal Jargon

Trademark law is full of highly specific, nuanced terms that may be unfamiliar to most founders. When you come across one of these legal terms, Gemini can help explain it in plain language. Here’s an example prompt:

Explain the concept of “Likelihood of Confusion” in trademark law as if I am a business owner with no legal background. What does “likelihood of confusion” mean, and how do trademark examiners evaluate it?

In this case, Gemini may explain that a trademark application can be rejected even if it is not 100% identical to an existing trademark, as long as consumers might mistakenly believe that your products or services are being delivered by an existing company.

Step 4: Organize Your Materials

You want to make your trademark attorney’s job as simple as possible for two reasons: 1) When your attorney has all relevant assets, accurate information about your products and services, and clear examples of how the mark is being used, it reduces the odds of misunderstandings and paves the path for a smoother application process; and 2) Most lawyers bill by the hour.

Instead of spending the first 30 minutes of your consultation digging through your files, take a moment to gather and organize materials beforehand. Gemini can help.

Try this prompt: I am preparing for my first meeting with a trademark attorney. Create a checklist of the exact business assets, dates of first use, URLs, and brand materials I need to gather beforehand so I don’t waste billable hours.

By putting in this preparation work at the beginning of the process, you can avoid delays, reduce unnecessary legal fees, and ultimately secure the trademark protection you need to build a lasting business.
